Items.Authors: Ismam Abu, Fulvio Gianotti, Andrea Bulgarelli, Pietro Bruno, Luca Castaldini, Isaias Huerta, Vito Conforti, Mattia Corpora, Alessandro Costa, Ambra Di Piano, Federico Fiordoliva, Valentina Fioretti, Stefano Gallozzi, Andrea Giuliani, Alessandro Grillo, Federico Incardona, Marcello Lodi, Saverio Lombardi, Fabrizio Lucarelli, Andrea Mandica, Emilio Mastriani, Kevin Munari, Nicolò Parmiggiani, Giovanni Pareschi, Valerio Pastore, Federico Russo, Pierluca Sangiorgi, Salvatore Scuderi, Alessandro Tacchini, Gino Tosti, Sebastiano Spinello
Items.Title: Integration of the ICT Kubernetes Cluster with the SCADA System for the ASTRI Mini-Array Project
Items.Abstract: The ASTRI Mini-Array is an INAF-led project deploying nine dual-mirror Cherenkov telescopes for very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy. Seven telescopes are installed, and two are already acquiring Cherenkov data during commissioning. A dedicated ICT infrastructure supports installation and operations, integrating network services, a virtualization platform, a computing cluster, distributed storage, and auxiliary systems.  Kubernetes is adopted as the computing platform to provide scalability, resilience, and efficient orchestration of SCADA subsystems, including Kafka, Cassandra, MongoDB, and InfluxDB, together with ASTRI-specific monitoring and data-quality services. CI/CD pipelines with integrated GitLab runners enable reproducible and traceable software releases.  This contribution presents the Kubernetes integration with operational services, and key challenges such as containerizing ACS and enabling communication between virtualized and containerized components.

Items.Authors: Tianzhu Hu
Items.Title: Intelligent Thermal and Airflow Control Methods for Optical Telescope Domes
Items.Abstract: The image quality of large-aperture optical telescopes is extremely sensitive to small variations in dome seeing. Effective control of dome temperature and airflow is therefore essential, yet current strategies rely on numerical simulations that cannot feasibly explore the vast state space of large telescope domes with multiple heat sources and complex environmental-control devices. We present an AI-assisted dome-seeing optimization framework that integrates laser-based dome-seeing monitoring, numerical thermal simulation, and reinforcement learning. We first establish the relationship between dome seeing and thermal gradients, then use simulation-generated temperature fields to train a reinforcement-learning controller, which is further improved via online learning. This report presents our recent progress and preliminary image-quality optimization results obtained on the LAMOST telescope.

Items.Authors: Xiaodong Ren, Jón E. Guðmundsson
Items.Title: Investigating polarization effects in the Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope using a novel physical optics code
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope (SO LAT) is designed to deliver high-fidelity measurements of cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization, and therefore requires precise control and modeling of instrumental polarization across a wide field of view. We present an efficient Physical Optics (PO) framework that combines a two-step PO method for the large crossed-Dragone reflector with a hybrid-PO analysis for the cold refractive optical tubes. This approach captures the frequency-dependent transmission and polarization properties of lenses with sub-wavelength structures, such as the silicon lenses used on SO LAT. Using the resulting beams and Mueller-matrix patterns across the focal plane, we quantify key polarization systematics, including temperature-to-polarization leakage and Q/U mixing arising from optical non-idealities.

Items.Authors: Joel Payne, Joseph Rounsaville, Jason N. Worden, Jonathan Steiner, Max Davis, Ellie O'Brien, Michael Dahler, John S. Hudek, Adam Vandenberg, Truman Wold, Rick Johnston, Justin Ballard, Erin Roberts, Dennis McBride, Grant Hill, Derek Park, Steve Baca, Adan Rodrigues, Jerez Tehero, Chris Martins, James Chong, Robert Harrington, Lauren Simmons, John Valliant, Danny Baldwin, Hamza Elwir, Tod Von Boeckmann, Ed Wetherell, Zach Tadio, Eric Levine, Dennis Patterson, Daniel Orr, Ben McCarney
Items.Title: Investigation and Recovery from a Failed Wire Rope Supporting the Keck II Telescope Top Shutter
Items.Abstract: On July 4, 2025, a significant failure of the Keck II primary (top) shutter occurred. Eight wire rope cables, each 5/8” steel, support the ~90,000 lbm shutter. One of the wire ropes broke catastrophically rendering the shutter (and therefore telescope) inoperable. The cause was unclear, risks uncertain, and the path forward not obvious.     This paper is a case study analyzing failure of a critical, dynamic structure. It details both investigation and recovery from the failure. A total of 51 nights were lost with the telescope unable to observe. Topics will include: 1) Background and sequence of events leading up to the failure. 2) Safety measures the team took to ensure no harm to people or the system. 3) Root cause diagnosis. 4) Recovery measures enabling a return to observation. 5) Improvements to the process for tensioning the wire ropes. 6) Longer-term strategies and recommendations on instrumentation that could have potentially detected and prevented the failure.

Items.Authors: Ritika Singh, Christian Pommranz, Michael Freyberg, Emanuele Perinati, Christoph Tenzer, Andrea Santangelo
Items.Title: Investigation of XMM-Newton mirror shell misalignment using ray-tracing
Items.Abstract: Stray light in X-ray telescopes such as XMM-Newton and eROSITA is a well-recognized source of systematic issue, arising primarily from singly reflected photons from either the hyperbolic or parabolic sections of the Wolter-I mirror. Because these instruments employ tightly nested mirror assemblies, isolating a sole contribution to the effective area loss from individual elements using ray-tracing requires a tool capable of accurately simulating such a complex optical design. In this work, we use MARXS (Multi Architecture Raytrace Xray mission Simulator), a Python compatible version of NASA’s MARX (Model of AXAF Response to X-ray) software developed for the Chandra X-ray Observatory. We adapt MARXS to build a detailed simulation of the XMM-Newton mirror module, that will be used to investigate the impact of shell misalignments on the effective area of the instrument.

Items.Authors: Aleksandar Shulevski, Maaijke Mevuis, Pietro Zucca, Emanuella Orru, Alan Wood, Gareth Dorrian
Items.Title: Ionospheric monitoring with LOFAR
Items.Abstract: One key aspect of improving the observational efficiency of the upgraded LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) telescope is monitoring the observing conditions, especially at the lowest observing frequencies, to ascertain which science programs can get time on sky. Space weather related ionospheric activity and solar bursts especially at solar maximum can severely limit useful observing windows.    We aim to monitor the ionosphere continuously during operations and construct a metric based (among other inputs) on the ionospheric scintillation index (S4) as well as monitoring solar activity using the observing setup and analysis pipelines developed as part of the Incremental Development Of LOFAR for Space weather (IDOLS) project.    I will present the initial monitoring results obtained during LOFAR commissioning. LOFAR station data reduction and the corresponding metrics will be discussed, as well the plans for their integration into the telescope monitoring and scheduling system (TMSS).

Items.Authors: Armin Silber
Items.Title: Keeping solar energy switched on during nighttime operation. The way forward to a sustainable and green observatory
Items.Abstract: The widespread discussion about renewable energy for Observatories is driven by the commitment to increase the efficiency of energy use hence to save on operational budgets and to reduce the carbon footprint. One of the motivation blockers to invest in sustainable technologies is an existing working infrastructure. In this contribution we will demonstrate on the example of the La Silla Observatory, that the investment is paying off in a reasonable time-frame, when guided by a profound analysis to identify synergies between different energy-consumers. The transformation of a traditional astronomical facility into a sustainable Observatory might inspire the global astronomical community to consider eco-friendly approaches highlighting the benefits of sustainability in reducing operational costs and minimizing the ecological footprint.

Items.Authors: Bin Ma
Items.Title: Laboratory and On-sky Testing of Infrared Camera Candidates for a 40 cm Telescope at Dome A, Antarctica
Items.Abstract: Dome A, Antarctica is recognized as a leading ground-based site for infrared astronomy due to its extremely cold, dry and stable atmosphere. Following the initial deployment of a 15cm Antarctic InfraRed Binocular Telescope (AIRBT) with 640×512 InGaAs cameras in 2023, we are developing a second-generation system with a 40 cm telescope. Two infrared camera options are under evaluation: a 1280×1024 InGaAs camera for a larger field of view, and a 640×512 HgCdTe camera for sensitivity at longer wavelengths. We will perform laboratory tests to measure the fundamental detector properties of both cameras. Then each camera will be integrated with the 40cm telescope for on-sky testing in China. The final camera selection will be based on these technical assessments, aligned with specific scientific objectives for the Dome A.

Items.Authors: Laura Mascetti
Items.Title: Lessons from ESO Phase 3: confronting the challenges of a decade-old system
Items.Abstract: The ESO Phase3 system, the dedicated channel for submitting homogeneous, science-ready data products to the ESO Archive, has become a critical pillar and an invaluable resource for the scientific community. However, its 2016 architecture is now challenged by hardware and software obsolescence, by the steadily growing data volumes from next-generation surveys and increasing demands to support novel data formats.   This presentation details the shortcomings and the necessity of transforming the Phase3 system into a flexible, scalable, and future-proof platform. We illustrate the need for an implementation plan centred on modernising the core infrastructure, enhancing the user experience, and introducing key new capabilities. Even well-established platforms must evolve to meet growing scientific and technical demands, while acknowledging the practical challenges and uncertainties of implementing such changes in real time.

Items.Authors: Ellie O'Brien, Shui Hung Kwok
Items.Title: Lifecycle Analysis for Critical Systems at Large Astronomical Observatories
Items.Abstract: During 30 years of constant operation, the mechanical components which support and drive the Keck Telescope and Dome systems are undergoing a transition from routine operations and maintenance to rapid run out and obsolescence. Sustaining and upgrading these systems are necessary to ensure the ongoing operation of the facility to achieve the scientific goals of the Keck observing community. This paper will serve as a case study to analyze the Telescope Azimuth, Elevation and Dome Azimuth drive systems. Lifecycle, load and fatigue parameters will be assessed for decades of mechanism and system motion data. A failure mode, effects and criticality analysis (FMECA) coupled with a mean time to failure (MTTF) analysis will be used to define new preventative maintenance and replacement intervals during rapid run out. The adaption of industry standard asset management and reliability engineering processes to suit the Keck Observatory application will be discussed.

Items.Authors: Gabriel González Rial, José Javier Díaz García, Francisco Javier Casas Reinares, Ricardo Tanausú Génova Santos
Items.Title: Litebird TMCS readout electronics: challenges, progress, and outlook
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a next-generation space mission aimed at producing highly sensitive, full-sky maps of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarization. Spain is contributing to the mission's operations and analysis, as well as the technological development of the payload through the Temperature Monitoring and Compensation System (TMCS). The TMCS is crucial for monitoring and stabilizing the thermal environment of the Transition Edge Sensor (TES) detectors. These detectors operate near 100 mK, requiring thermal stability at the level of a few micro-kelvin (or less), which is a major technical challenge. Current prototyping focuses on developing and validating the dedicated TMCS readout electronics through targeted tests and a complete readout chain implementation. The associated paper will summarize the stability requirements, TMCS initial approach and the results from the validation campaign.

Items.Authors: Riccardo Claudi, Adriano Ghedina, Lorenzo Cabona, Monica Rainer, Stefania Stefani, Andrea Tozzi, Riccardo Ciantini, Andrea Chiodini, Emanuele Pace, Scigè John Liù
Items.Title: LOCNES Telescope Commissioning and first observations
Items.Abstract: LOCNES (LOw Cost NIR Extended Solar) telescope is a newly installed solar telescope at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG). It has been specifically developed to examine the Sun as a star in the near-infrared spectrum (from 900 nm to 2.4 micron), with the main scientific aim of understanding how the Sun's surface irregularities and activity influence radial velocity measurements and provide hints for achieving optimal radial velocity corrections. The concept and the measurements of the instrument's performance, both in the laboratory and during on-sky testing, conducted throughout the intensive testing phase of LOCNES, will be presented.  Furthermore, we provide an overview of the initial scientific results from the science verification of LOCNES.   In conclusion, we emphasize the significant role that LOCNES can play in conjunction with other studies of the Sun as a star over the next decade, particularly in the field of extrasolar planets.

Items.Authors: Anne-Laure L. Cheffot, Davide Orsucci, Lisa Bardou
Items.Title: Long-baseline infrared interferometry using quantum communication networks in Europe
Items.Abstract: In recent years, several publications have suggested that technologies and infrastructure developed for quantum communication could be leveraged to enable long-baseline interferometry. In this article, we provide an overview of the proposed technologies, their current capabilities, and the infrastructure being deployed across Europe. We examine how long-baseline infrared interferometry can benefit from these systems and which adaptations would be necessary to meet its specific requirements.

Items.Authors: HyeYun Park, Kshitija Kelkar, Ignacio Sevilla-Noarbe, Laura Toribio San Cipriano, Petr Kubánek, Bruno Quint, Brian Stalder, Tiago Ribeiro
Items.Title: M1M3 dynamic performance – stability & actuation during operations
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is preparing to commence the Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Following integration of the complete Simonyi Survey Telescope, dynamic tests of the M1M3 primary/tertiary mirror assembly were conducted to verify operational readiness with respect to safety, stability, and image quality. The 8.4 m, 17 ton M1M3 system employs 156 force actuators and six hardpoint actuators to counteract gravitational and inertial loads while the telescope executes slews of order 1 degree per second even at 10 % of its speed, and must settle within 5 seconds between visits. Precisely coordinating the actuator forces under these high-speed motions is a significant control challenge. Test activities characterized hardpoint force control, assessed dynamical stability during slews and tracking, and evaluated force-actuator performance across a range of velocities and acceleration profiles consistent with the telescope’s expected operational envelope.

Items.Authors: Kirtan P. Dixit, Danielle N. Gurgew, Panini S. Singam, Jessica A. Gaskin, Stephen D. Bongiorno, Nicholas E. Thomas, David D. Smith
Items.Title: Machine learning-based inverse design of X-ray multilayers for high energy astrophysics missions
Items.Abstract: An end-to-end machine-learning framework is under development to design depth-graded multilayer (DGM) coatings for full-shell grazing-incidence optics from science requirements. The pipeline takes as input a target effective-area–versus–energy curve, telescope geometry, grazing-angle range and number of mirror shells, and works backwards to find a coating design for each shell so that the combined optic reproduces the requested response. A fast physics-based reflectivity calculator is coupled to machine-learning models that propose DGM recipes, followed by an optimization stage that adjusts shell reflectivities to better match the target effective area. Initial studies focus on hard X-ray telescope designs, and the framework is structured to extend to other energy bands and optical layouts. The goal is a practical tool that shortens multilayer optimization time and clarifies trade-offs between science performance, coating complexity and fabrication limits for future space telescopes.

Items.Authors: Benoit Borguet, Christian Bastin, Vincent Moreau, Brunella Carlomagno, Maxime Quesnel, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Jochem van der Maas, Lucie Violleau
Items.Title: MADOCS: a high-speed and robust adaptive optics control system for optical communications
Items.Abstract: We present MADOCS, a high-speed adaptive optics (AO) system derived from the SALTO demonstrator and engineered for free-space optical communication on a 1-m-class telescope. Designed to operate outside traditional observatory conditions, the system must accommodate rapid satellite slews and therefore achieve higher control bandwidths than typical AO used in astronomy. MADOCS employs two independent control loops: a 4 kHz tip–tilt loop using a fast-steering mirror for pointing stabilization, and a 2.5 kHz deformable-mirror loop for higher-order correction. Laboratory evaluations under controlled turbulence conditions demonstrate stable, low-latency closed-loop operation. By the time of the conference, we expect to present on-sky results showing the practical transfer of astronomical AO techniques to the more demanding temporal and pointing-stability requirements of optical communication.

Items.Authors: Helen M. McGregor, Jon Moller, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Zahoor, Zhemin Cai, Jon Lawrence, Celestina Lacombe, Jessica Zheng, Chris Coote, Lew Waller, Nirmala Kunwar, Tony Farrell, Tayyaba Zafar, Michael Goodwin, Vitor Neves Hartmann
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT, conceptual design for the fibre positioner
Items.Abstract: MANIFEST is a fibre-positioning system for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) that will feed light from hundreds of deployable probes into high- and medium-resolution spectrographs, including G-CLEF and GMACS, across 350–1000 nm and future infrared instruments. Initially covering the corrected 14′ field-of-view, MANIFEST will later expand to the full 20′ field-of-view. It offers single fibres, multiple integral-field-units, and image-slicing for enhanced resolution and wavelength coverage. Key capabilities include high multiplexing, simultaneous multi-instrument observations, and adaptability for future instruments. Using a pick-and-place robotic system, MANIFEST will significantly boost GMT’s survey efficiency and scientific productivity. In this paper we present the conceptual design overview for MANIFEST.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Moller, Christopher Coote, Jessica Zheng, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Zahoor, Zhemin Cai, Helen McGregor, Jon Lawrence, Celestina Lacombe
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT, conceptual opto-mechanical design
Items.Abstract: This paper describes the current conceptual design of the opto-mechanical components, mechanisms and general instrument architecture that enable MANIFEST to perform effectively under the Giant Magellan Telescope’s operational conditions. The instrument features several hundred probes connected to optical fibres precisely positioned over a curved field plate, which requires to change position to allow four pick-and-place robots to reach the probes and deploy them in different field configurations. The science observations are performed once the field plate is positioned at the focal plane where a large Field Lens corrects and focuses the light into the micro lens array and prism fitted inside each probe.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Moller, Zhemin Cai, Dylan Simpfendorfer, Jahanzaib Jahoor, Helen McGregor, Jon Lawrence, Celestina Lacombe
Items.Title: MANIFEST for GMT, structural design during CoDR phase
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive finite element analysis (FEA) of the updated MANIFEST mechanical architecture for the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT). Following the transition from Starbug robots to a pick-and-place fiber positioning system, the design now incorporates a curved metal field plate, magnetic fiber buttons, four robotic arms and mechanisms to move the field plate between operating positions. These structural changes introduce new mechanical challenges requiring validation across gravity, thermal, and dynamic loading conditions. Detailed FEA models were developed to evaluate deformation, stress, and modal behaviour for the field plate, corrector field lens group, and the integrated system. Simulations include gravity-induced displacement under multiple orientations, thermal expansion across operational and survival ranges, and dynamic response under varying preload conditions

Items.Authors: Marcial Becerril Tapia, Mayank Baghoria, Peter Barry, Thomas Brien, Simon Doyle, Christopher Dunscombe, Harry Gordon-Moys, Alan Manning, Sam Rowe, Chris Woodhead
Items.Title: Mapping large CMB-KID arrays through LED scanner
Items.Abstract: Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) are widely used in the development of large-format cameras in the millimetre/far-infrared range. Due to minor non-uniformities inherent in their manufacturing, there are uncontrolled variations in the detectors' resonance frequencies, leading to overlaps or interactions between two or more resonators. Modifying the resonance frequencies of one or more resonators by controlled changes in their capacitance can correct these collisions. This work presents the development and performance of a cryogenic LED scanner for mapping detectors. We show the latest results from mapping large KID arrays of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) detectors (>400), characterising their resonator properties, including quality factors and dispersion of resonance frequencies. Having the resonator collisions located, we lithographically trim their capacitors, decoupling the resonances and improving array yield.

Items.Authors: Jesse Cranney, Julien Bernard, Francois Rigaut, David Brodrick, Valentina Viotto, Guido Agapito, Stefan Ströbele
Items.Title: MAVIS: adaptive optics control principles
Items.Abstract: The MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph (MAVIS) has recently reached its final design, and is due to be deployed on the Very Large Telescope (UT4) in the early 2030s. We present a summary of the control principles for MAVIS at the final design stage, including the real time control approach for the MCAO and LGS jitter loop, and auxiliary control tasks such as LGS range compensation and pupil steering.

Items.Authors: Amirhossein Kermani, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Marco Riva, Matteo Genoni, Alessio Zanutta, Lorenzo Cabona, Chiara Selmi, Andrea Balestra, Matteo de Magistris
Items.Title: MBSE and astronomical instrument design: latest updates and future developments in INAF and the Italian community
Items.Abstract: In recent years, INAF has embarked on large ESO projects such as MORFEO, ANDES for the ELT, and CUBES for the VLT. The technical complexity of such projects, coupled with the number of people and institutions involved in their design, makes their system-level management almost impossible when addressed using the traditional document-based approach. This issue has been addressed by adopting Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), in which models serve as the single source of truth for the system, thereby dramatically improving reliability, univocity, and traceability.  The AstroMBSE methodology has been developed to support systems engineering tasks. Its tools have been applied to various projects, resulting in clearer, more efficient, and more reliable development processes.  New branches are currently exploring support for the early stages of design. The application of AI and ML is another open topic to understand where they can be effectively applied and how.

Items.Authors: Zain Azam, Ryan Dungee, Ting Li, Aditya Khandelwal, Sarik Jeram
Items.Title: Measuring the stability of readout performance for the OrcaQuest CMOS imaging censor
Items.Abstract: The OrcaQuest CMOS sensor by Hamamatsu Photonics has been found to exhibit changes in bias frame values over time. This effect is characterized through the various exposure tests and data reduction pipelines detailed in this report, which can be used to apply the appropriate bias frames under a range of environmental conditions. We also explore the effect of a readout card on readout speed and noise performance under fast camera capture rates. Such data can be used to provide more consistent measures of pixel gain, linearity, and low light images.

Items.Authors: Lawrence Bissell, Éamonn J. Harvey, Alastair Macleod, Valentina Oyarzun, Daniel Dicken, Katherine Morris, Philip Parr-Burman, Alistair Glasse, Felix Bettonvil, Bernhard Brandl
Items.Title: METIS for ELT: optical alignment and testing of the IFU of the LM-band spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The METIS LMS (LM-band Spectrograph) is a high-resolution (R>100,000) mid-infrared integral field spectrograph for the ESO ELT. The instrument provides the capability to measure instantaneous spectra across a 0.577 x 0.897 arcsecond field-of-view with a spatial sampling of 8.2-9.1 mas using an image slicing IFU. This paper presents the optical testing and alignment performed for the IFU sub-system including: the detailed characterisation of the image slicing mirror array; an overview of the optical alignment strategy employed during the AIT process, and results of the optical testing performed on the integrated sub-system.

Items.Authors: Peter Bizenberger, Harald Baumeister, Bernhard Brandl, M. Concepcion Cardenas Vazquez, Eduardo Chamorro, Dennis Dolkins, Silvia Scheithauer, Takashi Sukegawa
Items.Title: METIS: Grism spectroscopy in the mid-IR
Items.Abstract: METIS, the Mid-infrared ELT Imager and Spectrograph for the ELT offers mid-infrared grism spectroscopy in the atmospheric L, M & N bands. We describe the optical design, the cryogenic mounting, manufacturing and verification results of these three grisms. They have been developed and produced in close collaboration with CANON, Japan.   Particularly, wavefront and transmission measurements at component level are presented. Setup of test stands and results of verification are outlined and presented. Key parameter is the anti-reflection coating in order to achieve a high throughput with Germanium substrates.

Items.Authors: Ralf K. Heilmann, Alexander R. Bruccoleri, Shiva Mudide, Mark L. Schattenburg
Items.Title: Metrology and diffraction efficiency improvements for ultra-high aspect ratio, blazed soft x-ray transmission gratings
Items.Abstract: Critical-angle transmission (CAT) gratings are blazed gratings for high resolving power x-ray spectroscopy in mission concepts such as Arcus or Lynx addressing high-priority Astro2020 science goals. We demonstrated R ~ 1.2e4 for co-aligned CAT gratings. Diffraction efficiency (DE) can be improved via thinning of grating bars, optimizing bar profiles and tilt, and reducing sidewall roughness and support structures. Bar profiles and tilt are initially set in the deep reactive-ion etch (DRIE) step during fabrication. We developed fast and non-destructive profile and tilt metrology based on Mueller matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry (MMSE) and machine learning (ML) that can be used right after the DRIE step. The following KOH polish ideally reduces scalloping and results in smooth bar sidewalls. We plan to apply MMSE/ML to post-KOH bars to optimize KOH etch parameters next. We report on the x-ray DE of the latest CAT gratings with reduced supports and oxidation/HF-thinned bars.

Items.Authors: Simon R. Bandler
Items.Title: Microcalorimeter design options for the Lynx2030 X-ray Observatory
Items.Abstract: Lynx2030 is an X-ray telescope concept for the next NASA Astrophysics Decadal Survey, evolving from the 2020 Lynx mission concept. A key instrument is the Lynx X-ray Microcalorimeter (LXM), combining microcalorimeter arrays with high-resolution X-ray optics. The baseline uses transition-edge sensors (TES), with metallic magnetic calorimeters (MMC) as an alternative. The ~100-kilopixel array employs thermal sensors reading sub-arrays of 20-25 pixels to manage readout complexity. LXM will provide unprecedented diagnostics of distant structures, enabling detailed cosmic feedback studies. We describe technological progress since the last Decadal Survey, discuss focal plane design modifications responding to updated science requirements, examine multiplexed readout advances, and analyze implications for cooling power and mechanical assembly design.

Items.Authors: Mohammad A. Khan, Al Alexis
Items.Title: Mid-infrared laser heterodyne radiometer for remote sensing and planetary applications
Items.Abstract: Laser heterodyne radiometry (LHR) is primarily used for remote sensing of atmospheric column and molecular densities, specifically trace gases. The technique utilizes the mixing of two radiations: one is sunlight, and the other is a local oscillator, typically a laser tuned to spectral line transitions of interest. In this paper, we demonstrate a mid-infrared coupled LHR system to quantify molecular rotational-vibrational line transitions of methane and water vapor in the spectral region of 3.7 μm and 6.8 μm. We used integrated wavelength-modulation spectroscopy to discriminate overlapping line transitions, thereby improving the fit of the speed-dependent Hartmann-Tran Profile (HTP) lineshape models. The laboratory-based instrumentation can be field-deployed for earth science and planetary applications by simply modifying the solar tracker modules.

Items.Authors: Louis Gemmerlé, Manon Lallement, Jean-Philippe Berger, Guillermo Martin, Stéphane Curaba, Pierre R. Labeye
Items.Title: MILENE: an interferometric test bench for mid infrared photonic integrated circuits
Items.Abstract: Nulling interferometry allows us to benefit from a high angular resolution, as well as the capability to observe exoplanets with higher planet-to-star flux ratio through coherent cancellation of the flux from the star. Using photonic integrated circuits (PIC) for the aperture recombination function has the potential to improve the instrument performance. We present a dedicated four beam interferometric bench to characterise these PICs. Its design permits the consideration of an upgrade to eight interferometric channels, opening the way to the characterisation of up-to-eight-telescope recombination PICs. The uniformity of the injection is heightened by the development of a telecentric injection system. Moreover, in order to achieve deep null values, a stringent precision in controlling the phase, intensity and polarisation of each individual beam is required. We present the error budget and the characterisation of various control elements used on the bench.

Items.Authors: John Di Miceli
Items.Title: Mitigating Risk at Remote Astronomical Facilities: Emergency Preparedness Framework at the MMT Observatory
Items.Abstract: The MMT Observatory operates in a remote, high-altitude environment at the summit of Mt. Hopkins where limited access, severe weather, forest-fire risk, and extended transport times to definitive medical care create significant operational challenges. This paper presents the emergency preparedness framework developed at the MMT to enhance safety and mitigate these risks during scientific operations. Key components include mountain-specific emergency action plans covering medical incidents, wildfires, severe weather, and communication limitations. Enhanced wilderness-oriented first aid capabilities, infrastructure and personnel protection strategies, strengthened partnerships with regional agencies, and diversified communication pathways collectively minimize the impact of emergencies on observatory operations. These measures offer a practical model for improving safety and operational resilience at remote astronomical facilities.

Items.Authors: Pedro Escárate, Christopher Zamorano, Juan C. Agüero
Items.Title: Model predictive control for adaptive optics
Items.Abstract: Stochastic disturbances such as atmospheric turbulence and vibrations significantly degrade the performance of Adaptive Optics (AO) systems in modern astronomical instruments, including coronagraph-based exoplanet imagers and extreme AO architectures. This work presents a Model Predictive Control (MPC) strategy designed to improve rejection of these disturbances and enhance image stability and contrast. The approach relies on a stochastic state-space model of wavefront dynamics, including disturbances characterized in the spectral domain via log-Whittle likelihood estimation. Experimental simulations applied to tip/tilt modes demonstrate superior disturbance mitigation compared with standard AO controllers. Future efforts focus on real-time implementation on a large number of Zernike modes to meet the high-speed requirements of next-generation telescopes.

Items.Authors: Mehmet Kuruçolak, Derya Öztürk Çetni, Elif YAĞMUR KURUÇOLAK, Cahit Yeşilyaprak
Items.Title: Model-based systems engineering for early concept studies of the DAG400 active optics wavefront sensor
Items.Abstract: This study focuses on the impact of applying a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) approach during the early conceptual development of the Active Optics Wavefront Sensor (aOWFS). On the diffraction limited Nasmyth platform, the aOWFS shares optical paths, mechanical mounting points, and data access channels with the existing optical systems on the platform. This situation introduces coupled optical and mechanical constraints on available volume, alignment, cabling, vibration, and thermal conditions, making it difficult to manage the system consistently using document-based descriptions alone. In this work, these multidisciplinary constraints are captured within a single, integrated system model using an MBSE approach, allowing potential integration conflicts to be made visible at an early stage. The resulting model functions as a reference model for the aOWFS and for future Nasmyth instruments with similar interface structures.

Items.Authors: Kyle Lanclos, William T. S. Deich, Paul Richards, John I. Bailey, Prakriti Gupta, Matthew Brown, Aaron Hunter, Dusty Reichwein
Items.Title: Modern KTL: the next generation of interprocess communications at W. M. Keck Observatory
Items.Abstract: Nearing completion in 2025 at W. M. Keck Observatory (WMKO), the modern KTL (mKTL) interprocess communications standard is positioned as the successor to the Keck Task Library (KTL) applications programming interface (API), a standard at the core of all instrument and telescope operations at WMKO for more than 30 years, a source of stability and common functionality spanning at least three major shifts in computing infrastructure (VME crates, UNIX, and Linux) during that time.    The main goals of the mKTL initiative are to improve upon the functionality and performance of KTL while significantly lowering the barrier-to-entry for new developers and future maintainers, both of mKTL itself and programs relying on it. This paper covers the initial design and implementation of mKTL, starting with major design goals, proceeding to the first implementation in Python, and ending with our plans for future collaboration, development and deployment.

Items.Authors: Mrunmayi S. Deshpande, Tony Farrell, Satyam Mishra
Items.Title: Modernising Observatory Control: Integrating Legacy DRAMA with Next-Generation Instrumentation
Items.Abstract: The DRAMA (Distributed Real-Time AAO Monitor for Astronomy) framework was first developed at Anglo-Australian Observatory (AAO) in the early 1990s, Designed in C, C++, DRAMA provides a distributed, message-based control architecture. This robust design powers some of the most important astronomical instruments assembled at AAO — from the robot fibre positioner 2dF, spectrographs such as AAOmega, HERMES. DRAMA’s reliability and modular, task-oriented, real-time behaviour have also attracted international adoption. As new instruments are being developed at the AAO we are updating the DRAMA environment to meet modern software engineering and deployment practices. Recent efforts include containerising DRAMA using Docker and creating a modern Python interface. Currently, DRAMA continues to play an active role: it is used in the newly built KSPEC spectrograph for the KMTNet telescope, and forms the control architecture for the high-resolution spectrograph for the Devasthal Optical Telescope

Items.Authors: Andrew Lewis, Juan Cardenas, Gordon J. Stacey
Items.Title: Modernization of the control system of the Hartung-Boothroyd Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Hartung-Boothroyd Observatory (HBO), completed in 1975, is Cornell University’s undergraduate teaching and research facility for observational astronomy. The observatory houses a 25-inch f/13.5 Cassegrain reflector with an equatorial fork mounting, controlled electronically using a DOS-based program. This dated system has created a barrier to entry for modern users and teachers of astronomy at Cornell, and does not meet modern expectations for the widespread use cases of such an observatory. Therefore, we design and implement a simple modern control system for interacting with the telescope. The updated control system provides remote control capabilities for the telescope, built upon a subset of publicly available control protocols, allowing external applications to interface directly with the observatory. Furthermore, the revision improves the safety of the observatory through well-developed fault and limit checks, ensuring the telescope’s efficient and straightforward operation.

Items.Authors: José Leonardo Garcés Medina, Gerardo Lara, Carolina Keiman
Items.Title: Modernization of the FRIDA Cold Test Facility cryostat: Lessons learned from FRIDA and integration of modern supervisory technologies
Items.Abstract: The FRIDA Cold Test Facility (FCTF), a cryostat used extensively for the early validation of subsystems later integrated into the near-infrared instrument FRIDA, lacks many of the operational and safety features now standard in modern cryogenic systems. In contrast, the larger FRIDA cryostat -cycled more than ten times during integration- implements advanced house-keeping capabilities, including robust interlocks, structured data logging, automated thermal-cycle control, web-based monitoring, and messaging-bot alerts. We present a modernization of FCTF that incorporates these proven technologies into a new control architecture featuring a re-engineered control layer, an independent fail-safe interlock system, a supervisory server with automated procedures, real-time dashboards, and an alert-notification service. The upgrade transforms FCTF into a safer, more reliable, and more versatile platform for testing future cryogenic subsystems.

Items.Authors: Miguel Andrés Sánchez Carrasco, M. Carmen Pastor Morales, Juan Manuel Gómez López, Rosario Sanz Mesa, Julio F. Rodríguez Gómez, Nicolás Robles Muñoz, Francisco Lobón Villanueva, Sylvain Ranvier, Jean-Charles Matéo-Vélez, Rémi Pacaud, Michel Anciaux
Items.Title: Modular thermo-mechanical framework for agile prototyping of space instruments: the DUSTER case
Items.Abstract: The paper describes the thermo-mechanical framework developed for the DUSTER breadboard, aimed at integrating EMI-sensitive, high-voltage electronics in a configuration that remains practical for assembly and test. The enclosure is built from stacked aluminium frames supporting the DPU, the low- and high-voltage power supplies, and the sensor front-ends. Connector distribution was arranged to limit cable cross-routing and to keep kilovolt-level bias lines away from low-level analog paths. EMC control relies on conductive gaskets at the critical interfaces, while the thermal design follows a staged approach based on board-level conduction, internal heat links, and external baseplate coupling. This made it possible to introduce thermal improvements during laboratory testing without redesigning the enclosure.

Items.Authors: Francesco Di Mille, Marcelo Mora, Nicole David, Povilas Palunas
Items.Title: Monitoring Instrument Throughput at the Magellan Telescopes
Items.Abstract: We present an ongoing program to monitor the efficiency and throughput of the Magellan telescopes and their facility instruments. Standard stars and fields observed as part of routine operations are used to derive photometric zero points and spectroscopic efficiencies on a regular cadence. In parallel, the reflectivity of the primary, secondary, and tertiary mirrors is measured as part of the regular Magellan mirror-maintenance program, providing an estimate of the total telescope reflectivity. By correlating changes in mirror reflectivity and maintenance events with variations in instrument sensitivity, we link the state of the telescope optics directly to the overall response of the instrument suite. We present these correlations for individual instruments and discuss their use in tracking instrument health, validating performance after cleaning or recoating, and quantifying the long-term stability of system throughput across the facility.

Items.Authors: Chiara Di Prospero, Salvatore Lampitelli, Salvatore Savarese, Alfio Puglisi, Andrea Baruffolo, Giulio Capasso
Items.Title: MORFEO @ ELT - Prototyping activities of MORFEO Soft Real Time Computer towards ESO Final Design Review
Items.Abstract: MORFEO (Multi-conjugate adaptive Optics Relay For ELT Observations) is the post-focal adaptive optics module for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope. The instrument provides MCAO correction for two instruments: MICADO and HARMONI.  This paper details the prototyping activities for the MORFEO Soft Real Time Computer (SRTC), validating its architecture for stringent timing requirements and instrument functionalities, as presented at the ESO Final Design Review (FDR).  Using a hardware testbed and the ESO rtc-toolkit framework, three prototypes were developed:  1.A distributed full telemetry system managing high throughput via network separation (VLANs), real-time scheduling, and NUMA-aware resource allocation  2.Benchmarking of auxiliary loop algorithms in Python and C++, establishing the need for parallel computing and GPU acceleration  3.Customization of rtc-toolkit modules to meet instrument needs while preserving performance  The final SRTC design is based on these prototypes.

Items.Authors: Marco Falotico, Guido Agapito, Paolo Ciliegi, Giuseppe Notarstefano
Items.Title: MORFEO @ ELT: control strategies for tip-tilt compensation on Extremely Large Telescopes
Items.Abstract: MORFEO (Multi-conjugate adaptive Optics Relay For ELT Observations) is the post-focal adaptive optics  module for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope. The instrument provides MCAO correction for two instruments:  MICADO and HARMONI.  Compensation of Tip and Tilt modes of aberration is a key challenge on Extremely Large Telescopes like the  ELT, and on its Adaptive Optics module, MORFEO. Because of the large telescope structure and the wind  effects, Tip-Tilt disturbances have large power at very low frequencies, and may present resonant peaks related to  mechanical oscillations. In this work we analyze different control strategies for Tip-Tilt compensation, including  pure integrators, which may not be suited for accurate loop shaping, Infinite Impulse Response filters with online  gain optimization, and Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controllers. Frequency shaping of the LQG is investigated, to  recover stability margins of the closed loop in a measurement feedback scenario.

Items.Authors: Marco M. Riva, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Paolo Ciliegi, Andrea Di Rocco
Items.Title: MORFEO@ELT System Engineering toward FDR
Items.Abstract: Morfeo (Multi-conjugate adaptive Optics Relay For ELT Observations) is an adaptive optics module able to compensate the wavefront disturbances affective the scientific observation. It will be installed on the straight-through port of the telescope Nasmyth platform to serve the first-light instrument MICADO and with the provision for a future second instrument. The module underwent the Preliminary Design Review in 2021 and is starting now the FDR process.  In this paper we present a synthesis of the System Engineering approach adopted to manage the development of the instrument assessing the criticalities of phase C (final design) and beginning of phase D (Early procurement. We will discuss the evolution of the system engineering approach, identifying within the MBSE framework the evolution of the various modelling artefacts. towards the requirements. We will detail the criticalities of the system engineering with a particular focus onto the management of the interfaces between subsystem

Items.Authors: Julien Dejonghe, Nick Cvetojevic, Diane Chapuis Kerouanton, Tim Morris, Jürgen Schmoll, Nazim Ali Bharmal, Ian Lewis
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: concept proposal for a telescope beam simulator and alignment tool for MOSAIC
Items.Abstract: The ELT scale, combined with the accuracy required at visible and near-infrared wavelengths, leads to new challenges in terms of optical alignment.  MOSAIC uses the full field of view of the ELT, with 300 positioners redirecting light towards science paths. Four GLAO systems are able to acquire sub-fields and LED targets located on Focal Plane. Therefore, the sky is linked to the structure supporting the optics at focal plane. Nevertheless, as MOSAIC is dedicated to the observation of very faint objects, some science paths must work in a so-called “blind” mode: long exposures are necessary to get signal from the observed object. Active tracking on science beams is then difficult, and some challenging science requirements in term of pointing accuracy leads to define a co-alignment strategy, optically linking GLAO with the science paths.  This poster presents an alignment tool or ELT beam simulator concept, allowing high-precision optical alignment and proper look-up table building.

Items.Authors: Kacem El Hadi, Myriam Rodrigues, Diane Chapuis, Laurent Martin, Marc Jaquet, Alexandre Bozier, Bruno Castilho, Timothy J. Morris, Nazim Ali Bharmal, Ian J. Lewis, Markus Thurneysen, Maxime Rombach, Julien Dejonghe, Ana Pérez Calpena, Meghna Mohamed, Marie Larrieu, Michel Dupieux, Clément Hottier, Franck Ducret, Thomas Augusteijn, Gavin Dalton, Marísa Luisa García-Vargas, Alessandro Meoli, Roser Pello, Mathieu Puech, Jay Stephan, Ruben Jansen, Christian Surace
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: instrument AITV strategies
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the Muti-Object Spectrograph for the 39m ESO Extremely Large Telescope. The instrument development has recently been reorganized in different channels to be implemented progressively.  The Laboratoire d’Astrophysique de Marseille (LAM) is in charge of the instrument “Assembly, Integration, Test and Verification (AIT/V)” phases. AITV for AO instruments, in laboratory or at the telescope, always represent numerous technical challenges. We already started the preparation and planning for the instrument level AIT activities, from identification of needs, challenges, risks, to defining the the instrument AITV strategies.  In this paper, we present the state of this study, discuss the instrument integration & test options, all depending of the availability of any European AIT facility to host the full instrument. We describe a basline option with the full instrument test as well as new approach with distributed AIT activities and controlled remotely over different European sites.

Items.Authors: Zalpha Challita, Johan Floriot, Tony Pamplona, Alexandre Bozier, Yannick Charles, Anne-Sophie Hutter, Patrice Sanchez, Marísa Luisa García-Vargas, Kacem El Hadi, Jesús Gallego Maestro, Mathieu Puech, Roser Pello
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: overview of the MAIT strategy of an athermal camera prototype for the NIR-spectrograph
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object spectrograph (MOS) for the ESO 39m European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). The instrument is progressing in phase B2 since 2025. It presents multi-object and multi-integral field spectroscopy capabilities and combines visible and near-infrared channels, to observe from resolved stars up to the most distant galaxies. The two NIR-spectrographs (130K-80K) are part of the NIR-channel system led by the Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM, Spain). The current design includes four camera modules delivered by the Laboratoire d’Astrophysique de Marseille (LAM, France), two per spectrograph, ensuring the spectral coverage of the two observing bands J (0.95-1.34 μm) and H (1.43-1.8 μm). Each camera is equipped with Teledyne H4RG detectors (4kx4k, 15 μm pixels). This paper presents the MAIT strategy and development to verify the athermal concept of a cryogenic NIR camera prototype in relevant environment (ESO TRL5) and to anticipate the MAIT plan of the NIR cameras.

Items.Authors: Jay Stephan, Mathieu Puech, Ruben Sanchez-Janssen, Myriam Rodrigues, Armando Gil de Paz, Nicolas Laporte, Søren Larsen, Timothy J. Morris, Roser Pello, Thomas Augusteijn, Gavin Dalton, Kacem El Hadi, Marísa Luisa L. García-Vargas, Marie Larrieu, Alessandro Meoli, Hermine Schnetler, Christian Surace
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: status of science requirements and trade-off studies
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object spectrograph (MOS) for the 39-meter Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) of the European Southern Observatory (ESO). It offers unique capabilities in observing modes (single-object and integral field unit), multiplexing, wavelength coverage, and spectral resolution. Designed to operate in both the visible and near-infrared domains, MOSAIC maximizes coverage of the ELT focal plane (∼40 arcmin²) and is optimized to deliver the highest possible signal-to-noise ratio for the faintest sources—from stars in our Galaxy to galaxies at the epoch of reionization. This paper outlines the methodology used to translate top-level science requirements into instrument specifications and summarizes the key trade-off studies (e.g., GLAO sky coverage, science calibration, trace separation) carried out in preparation for the System Architecture Review, completed between April and June 2025.

Items.Authors: Bruno V. Castilho, Décio Ferreira, André G. Coutinho, Antonio B. Braulio Neto, Bruno S. Pinto, Leandro H. dos Santos, Lucimara Martins, Marc Jacquet, Alexandre Bozier, Diane Chapuis, Kacem El Hadi, Laurent Martin, Beatriz S. Barbuy, Thomas Augusteijn, Gavin B. Dalton, Marísa Luisa García-Vargas, Marie Larrieu, Alessandro Meoli, Roser Pello, Mathieu Puech, Myriam Rodrigues, Ruben Sanchez -Janssen, Hermine Schnetler, Jay Stephan, Christian Surace
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: the instrument core system design status
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC, the wide-field multi-object spectrograph for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is  advancing through Phase B2, where subsystem architectures mature toward the Preliminary  Design Review. Central to the Front-End channel is the Instrument Core System (ICOS), which  provides the mechanical support, alignment stability, and controlled rotation required by the  focal-plane assembly and the GLAO, ORSS, and CALEMOS subsystems. ICOS comprises a steel  Static Structure Module interfaced to the Nasmyth platform, a motorized Rotating Structure  Module that delivers field-rotation compensation with ≤0.095 mrad accuracy, and a Cable Wrap  Module enabling continuous ±180° motion. ICOS must include an alignment strategy capable of restoring the optical axis to the sub-100µm level required for injection efficiency and pupil stability. With refined interfaces and a mass near 13.4 t, ICOS is converging toward a robust preliminary design for Phase C.

Items.Authors: Nick Cvetojevic, Julien Dejonghe, Nicolas Mauclert, Paul Girard, Yan Caujolle, Olivier Boebion, Daniel Lecron, Stephane Lagarde, Diane Chapuis, Kacem El Hadi
Items.Title: MOSAIC at ELT: the optical relay sub-system (ORSS)
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object fibre spectrograph for ESO's 39-m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). It offers unique capabilities for a gigantic telescope in terms of multiplexing, wavelength coverage, and spectral resolution. One of MOSAIC’s observation modes is to position up to 8 independent fibre Integral Field Units (IFUs) anywhere withing the ~ 40 arcmin^2 field of view. To achieve this, each of MOSAIC’s positioners has an additional pick-off mirror that can redirect the light to the instrument’s edge and into the Optical Relay Sub-System (ORSS) modules that will inject in into the IFU fibre bundles, and enable the mIFU observation mode of MOSAIC. The module requirement is to ensure the image plane is at the correct place regardless of the targets position in the focal plane and must correct for up to 1m of optical path difference. In this paper we outline the latest optical and mechanical design of the ORSS module, their expected performance, and initial prototyping results.

Items.Authors: Ellen Schallig, Gavin Dalton, Ian J. Lewis, Louis Gabarra, Alec York, David Terrett, Diane Chapuis Kerouanton, Jürgen Schmoll, Thomas Augusteijn, Kacem El Hadi, Marísa Luisa García-Vargas, Marie Larrieu, Alessandro Meoli, Roser Pello, Mathieu Puech, Myriam Rodrigues, Rubén Sanchez-Janssen, Hermine Schnetler, Jay Stephan, Christian Surace
Items.Title: MOSAIC at the ELT: focal plane architecture and initial design
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object fibre spectrograph for ESO's 39-m Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). It offers unique capabilities for a gigantic telescope in terms of multiplexing, wavelength coverage and spectral resolution. MOSAIC covers the visible (0.39-0.95 microns) and NIR (0.95-1.8 microns) wavelength domains. It has been designed to cover the largest possible area (~40 arcmin²) on the ELT focal plane.  This paper describes the current architecture of MOSAIC’s Focal Plane subsystem, a curved support structure holding up to 300 SCARA robots that relay the light into fixed fibre bundles. We outline the design trade-offs for mass, thermal and gravitational stability and use of novel materials to achieve the required performance. We also report on the first results of prototyping activities relating to alignment strategies for the focal plane and its components. Lastly, we present the algorithms that manage the repositioning of the ensemble of robots between observations.

Items.Authors: Armando Gil de Paz, Ana Pérez Calpena, África Castillo Morales, Marisa García Vargas, Jesús Gallego, Ernesto Sánchez Blanco, Ramón Rodríguez Cardoso
Items.Title: MOSAIC for ELT: CALEMOS: calibration module for the ELT MOS
Items.Abstract: CALEMOS will be the Calibration Module for the MOSAIC instrument, currently under design for the European Large Telescope (ELT). It will provide illumination for the calibration of both its VIS and NIR channels. This MOSAIC sub-system shall incorporate artificial sources for spectral and flat calibration (and should fulfill the ESO-ELT light tightness requirements). Our flat calibrations will require of a continuous, uniform illumination aimed at providing both detector (pixel-to-pixel) and fiber (fiber-to-fiber) flat fielding. The large size of the calibration screen and high incidence angle of the CALEMOS beam are both challenging aspects of its design in terms of both homogeneity and irradiance. In this poster we will also describe the calibration model used to verify those instrument top-level requirements that depend on the performance of both CALEMOS and the MOSAIC calibration and observing strategies.

Items.Authors: Marísa Luisa L. García-Vargas, Ana Pérez-Calpena, Jesús Gallego Maestro, Yevgeniy Ivanisenko, Philippe Laporte, Isabelle Guinouard, Audrey Lanotte, Gerardo Veredas-Luque, Ernesto Sánchez-Blanco Mancera, Manuel Maldonado Medina, María Peñataro-Blanco, Zalpha Challita, Africa Castillo-Morales, José Miguel Ibáñez Mengual, Javier Piqueras López, Armando Gil de Paz, Francois Wildi, Cyril Pannetier, Thomas Augusteijn, Gavin Dalton, Kacem El Hadi, Marie Larrieu, Alessandro Meoli, Roser Pelló, Mathieu Puech, Myriam Rodrigues, Ruben Sanchez-janssen, Hermine Schnetler, Jay Stephan, Christian Surace
Items.Title: MOSAIC for ELT: NIR channel challenges and performance
Items.Abstract: MOSAIC is the multi-object, MOS, spectrograph for the ESO-ELT, designed for a wide range of scientific programs requiring high multiplexing capabilities. MOSAIC enables MOS observations with both low and high spectral resolution (LR and HR), utilizing the ELT’s entire Field of View (FoV, 40 arcmin²). It includes two channels, VIS (0.39 – 0.95 µm) and NIR (0.95 – 1.8 µm), with spectrographs on the Nasmyth platform, all fed by MOS fiber bundles and, in the case of the NIR channel, also by fibers from 8 mIFU sub-apertures. These channels span the full range with a spectral resolution of R ≥ 4,000 in a single exposure and, both also offer an HR mode (R ≥ 18,000). The NIR channel is being designed and developed by universities and research centers from Spain, France and Switzerland. This paper summarizes the challenges, organization and design status of MOSAIC NIR channel in the preliminary design stage.
